A unique rule asserts that no value appears twice in a column, which is how key columns are protected. It fails when duplicates exist and reports how many rows were involved. Duplicates usually mean one of two things. Either the file was exported twice and concatenated, in which case entire blocks of rows repeat and the row count is roughly double what it should be, or a join upstream multiplied records, in which case only some identifiers repeat and the rest of the row differs. Comparing the number of failed rows against the total row count is the quickest way to tell which happened.

A dataset in DataPact represents a data feed that your team receives repeatedly in the same shape, such as a monthly enrollment export or a weekly sales extract. You register it once from the Manage Datasets page by giving it a name, naming the team that sends it, and writing a short description of what the feed contains. The name has to be unique for the owner, so two people can each track a feed called Monthly Export without colliding. Registering a dataset does not upload any data. It only creates the subject that contracts and validation runs will attach to later. Until a contract exists, uploads for that dataset cannot be checked against anything.

Every dataset has exactly one owner, and ownership records who is accountable for the feed rather than who may look at it. Any signed-in user can view a dataset, search its contracts and read its violations. The owner is the person the team contacts when a file stops arriving or starts failing. Because ownership carries that responsibility, DataPact refuses to delete a user account that still owns datasets. The account has to be reassigned first, which prevents a single deletion from silently orphaning a feed and all of its history. Deactivating an account is the normal path when somebody leaves a team.

Telling the two resolutions apart is the central judgement in DataPact. A data issue means the file is wrong and somebody upstream should fix it. A contract update means reality changed and the rule should be rewritten. Three signals usually separate them. How many rows failed: a handful suggests data entry, a large and consistent block suggests a change in the business. Whether the offending values are all the same: one repeated new value suggests a new legitimate category, while scattered variants suggest typos. And whether the value looks plausible: a negative quantity is never legitimate, while a new campus code probably is.

As well as a username and password, DataPact supports signing in with a Google account. The Continue with Google button appears on both the login and sign-up pages, and the flow hands the account straight back to the application once Google confirms it. Google sign-in and password sign-in are alternatives rather than a sequence, so an account created one way does not need the other. If Google credentials have not been configured in the environment the button is replaced by a short note, and password sign-in continues to work normally, so a missing configuration never locks anybody out.

DataPact draws a deliberate line between its endpoints. The run-outcome summary is public: it returns three aggregate counts and no file names, dataset names or usernames, so it can be read without an account and used for charts or demonstrations. Every other endpoint requires a session. Protected pages redirect a signed-out browser to the login screen, which is the right behaviour for a person. Protected data endpoints instead return an unauthorised status with a short message, because a program calling an endpoint needs a clear refusal rather than a login page it cannot read.

DataPact can draft an explanation for a violation. Given one failed rule, it returns a plain sentence describing what appears to have happened, a proposed cause of either a data issue or an outdated contract, and a suggested next step. The feature exists because the judgement it supports is the slowest part of reviewing a failure: an analyst normally has to read the sample rows and reason about whether the business changed. The draft is a starting point, not a decision. The resolution field on a violation is only ever written by a person, and the suggestion cannot change it.
